sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Multiple myeloma (MM) develops in the hypoxic bone marrow (BM) microenvironment, which alters tumor behavior and immune responses. While hypoxia is known to directly suppress immune function, its effect on immunotherapy-relevant antigen expression and the MM secretome remains underexplored. Here, we investigated how hypoxia affects BCMA expression and BCMA-targeted CAR T cell responses.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: MM cells were cultured under normoxia (21% O₂) or hypoxia (1% O₂). BCMA surface and total expression were analyzed. Anti-BCMA CAR T cells were co-cultured with normoxic or hypoxic MM cells to assess cytotoxicity and cytokine release. Conditioned media and small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) were isolated, quantified, and RNA-profiled.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: MM cells cultured in hypoxia showed reduced BCMA surface and total protein expression, resulting in reduced CAR-mediated signaling. Importantly, the hypoxic tumor secretome further reduced BCMA levels and significantly impaired CAR T cell killing and cytokine production, which was partially reversible by γ-secretase inhibition. To dissect the suppressive nature of the hypoxic secretome, we identified an increase in small extracellular vesicle (sEV) release under hypoxia. RNA profiling of sEVs revealed a hypoxia-induced RNA signature with potential immunomodulatory roles.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study shows that hypoxia diminishes BCMA expression and enhances secretion of immunosuppressive factors, including sEVs, thereby limiting the efficacy of BCMA CAR T cell therapy in MM.

body.p: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a hematological malignancy characterized by the uncontrolled proliferation of plasma cells in the bone marrow (BM) [1]. The BM microenvironment is inherently hypoxic, with localized hypoxic niches that contribute to disease progression, metabolic reprogramming, and resistance to therapies such as proteasome inhibitors [1–3]. Recent therapeutic advances in MM have focused on immunotherapies, including mRNA vaccines, T-cell engagers (TCEs), monoclonal antibodies, and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy [4, 5], particularly those targeting B cell maturation antigen (BCMA). While the immunosuppressive effects of hypoxia on immune cell function are well established [6, 7], the specific impact of hypoxia on BCMA surface expression, the tumor’s secretome, and the subsequent responses to immunotherapy, remain poorly understood.

To investigate the effect of hypoxia on the expression of immunotherapy-relevant antigens in MM [8], we cultured RPMI-8226 and OPM-2 cell lines under hypoxic (1% O₂) or normoxic (21% O₂) conditions for 48 h. Hypoxia caused a reduction in CD138 and BCMA surface levels in RPMI-8226 (Fig. 1A) and OPM-2 cells (Sup Fig. 1A), whereas CD38 and B7-H3 remained stable. The decrease in BCMA was validated in additional cell lines (LP1 and MM1S), but was not observed in AMO1 cells (Fig. 1B, Sup Fig. 1B), reflecting cell line dependent heterogeneity. Similar variability was observed in primary MM samples (Fig. 1C). Total BCMA protein and mRNA levels under hypoxia were also examined by western blotting and qPCR (Sup Fig. 1C-D), confirming the observed reduction on protein level, but also on mRNA level in RPMI-8226 cells.

To assess the functional relevance of reduced BCMA surface expression for CAR T cell therapy, we co-cultured a BCMA CAR reporter (2D3) cell line with RPMI-8226 cells under hypoxic or normoxic conditions. BCMA CAR signaling was significantly reduced under hypoxia, indicating decreased antigen-specific activation (Fig. 1D). To determine whether this effect was intrinsic to BCMA levels or mediated by secreted factors, we preconditioned RPMI-8226 cells in normoxia or hypoxia for 48 h, followed by killing assays in normoxia with primary CAR T cells. Cells were cultured in either fresh RPMI-1640 medium, or in the secretome of normoxic or hypoxic MM cells (Fig. 1E), whereby cells placed in hypoxia or hypoxic secretome exhibited lower surface levels of BCMA (Fig. 1F). CAR T cells were accordingly significantly less effective at killing MM cells in the presence of the hypoxic secretome (Fig. 1G). Reduced cytokine secretion (IFN-γ, IL-2, and TNF-α) was observed in all conditions involving hypoxic myeloma cells, with the most pronounced suppression seen when tumor cells were cultured in the hypoxic secretome (Fig. 1H).

Previous studies have shown that hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), a key transcription factor in the hypoxic response, can promote γ-secretase activity [9], which in turn mediates BCMA cleavage from the cell surface [10, 11]. Measurement of soluble BCMA (sBCMA) levels in the culture supernatant showed similar levels in normoxia or hypoxia, despite decreased BCMA mRNA levels in hypoxic RPMI-8226 cells, suggesting increased BCMA shedding (Sup Fig. 1E). To test whether γ-secretase contributes to the hypoxia-mediated reduction in BCMA expression, we treated cells with the clinically tested γ-secretase inhibitor crenigacestat (LY3039478) [12]. Inhibition of γ-secretase not only partially restored BCMA levels (Sup Fig. 2A-B) and BCMA mediated CAR signaling (Sup Fig. 2C); it also partially restored CAR T cell-mediated killing (Fig. 1I, Sup Fig. 2D), supporting a contributing role of γ-secretases in hypoxic BCMA downregulation. However, the CAR T cell functionality was only partially restored, showing that CAR T cell dysfunction towards hypoxic myeloma cells is only partially mediated via decreased BCMA levels.

caption.p: Hypoxia reduces BCMA expression and impairs anti-BCMA CAR T cell function. A Surface expression of CD38, BCMA, B7-H3, and CD138 on RPMI-8226 cells cultured in normoxic (grey) or hypoxic (blue) conditions, measured after 48 h by flow cytometry. B Surface expression of BCMA on MM cells cultured in normoxic (grey) or hypoxic (blue) conditions, measured after 48 h by flow cytometry. From top to bottom: MM1S, LP1, AMO1, OPM-2 and RPMI-8226 cells. C Surface expression of BCMA on primary MM cells cultured under normoxic (grey) or hypoxic (blue) conditions, measured after 24 h by flow cytometry. (Left) representative example, (right) quantification of 5 patient samples. D Schematic of CAR-expressing 2D3 reporter cells, which upregulate GFP upon activation. Quantification of GFP⁺ 2D3 cells after co-culture with RPMI-8226 cells in normoxia or hypoxia (right). E Schematic experimental design of experiments performed in (E-H). RPMI-8226 cells were preconditioned for 48 h in normoxia or hypoxia, then co-cultured with CAR T cells in normoxia using either fresh medium, conditioned medium from normoxic cells, or conditioned medium from hypoxic cells. F BCMA surface expression on RPMI-8226 cells after 48 h normoxia or hypoxia and culture in the presence of the indicated secretome, as described in (E). G Cytotoxicity of anti-BCMA CAR T cells against normoxic (top) or hypoxic (bottom) preconditioned RPMI-8226 cells. Statistics shown for 1:1 effector-to-target (E: T) ratio (right) (n = 5). H Cytokine secretion (IFN-γ, IL-2, TNF-α) by anti-BCMA CAR T cells co-cultured with normoxic or hypoxic RPMI-8226 cells in the presence of the indicated secretome (n = 5). I Cytotoxicity of anti-BCMA CAR T cells against normoxic (top) or hypoxic (bottom) preconditioned RPMI-8226 cells after treatment with 100 nM of the γ-secretase inhibitor crenigacestat. Statistics shown for 1:1 effector-to-target (E: T) ratio. P-values are indicated. Statistical significance was assessed using a one-way ANOVA (n = 5) for panels D, G, H and I and a Student’s t-test for panel A. Experiments involving primary T cells (A, B,E, F) were performed using lymphocytes from at least three different healthy donors

body.p: To further assess the immunosuppressive effects of the hypoxic tumor secretome, we activated primary T cells using soluble CD3/CD28 agonists in the presence of the hypoxic or normoxic RPMI-8226 secretome. T cell proliferation, as measured by CFSE dilution, was significantly reduced in the presence of the hypoxic secretome (Fig. 2A). In addition, T cells exposed to the hypoxic secretome displayed increased surface expression of PD-1, suggesting a state of dysfunction or exhaustion (Fig. 2B). While the secretome comprises many factors (cytokines, metabolites, free proteins) that can alter T-cell responses, we focused on the release of small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) given its known role in solid tumors [13] but unknown role in MM (CAR) T cell dysfunction. We observed a more than 2-fold increase in sEVs released per cell under hypoxic conditions (Fig. 2C). To characterize the transcriptional cargo of these sEVs, we performed bulk RNA profiling on sEVs derived from HS5 stromal cells and RPMI-8226 MM cells under normoxic and hypoxic conditions. This enabled us to delineate a cancer/myeloma-specific RNA signature with potential T cell modulatory effects (Sup Fig. 3A). Additionally, differential analysis of sEVs derived from MM cells under normoxic versus hypoxic conditions (Fig. 2D) revealed a shift toward metabolic reprogramming, particularly enhanced anaerobic glucose metabolism, driven by (glycolytic) genes, including LDHA, PGK1, ENO1, and ALDOA. These hypoxia-associated alterations may contribute to T cell suppression, since glucose metabolism promotes the differentiation of T cells toward the effector phenotype, which is more prone to exhaustion and less proliferative compared to memory T cells [14]. To functionally validate this, we isolated RPMI-8226 derived sEVs under normoxic and hypoxic conditions and treated primary BCMA CAR T cells with them. We observed a decrease in central memory T cells after treatment with tumor derived sEVs, with a slightly more pronounced effect in T cells treated with hypoxic sEVs. These results suggest that tumor-derived sEVs may decrease CAR T cell persistence (Fig. 2E). A trend in increased expression of exhaustion markers was observed upon treatment with hypoxic sEVs (sup Fig. 3B). In contrast, no phenotypic effects were observed upon treatment with hypoxic stromal sEVs (sup Fig. 3C). Finally, we evaluated whether hypoxic sEVs impact CAR T cell function, and observed a small but significant decrease in their ability to kill MM cells (Fig. 2F).

caption.p: Hypoxic secretome and small EVs suppress T cell function. A T cell proliferation upon agonistic CD3/CD28 stimulation after 72 h in RPMI-1640 medium or in the presence of the secretome of normoxic/hypoxic RPMI-8226 cells. (Left) representative plots, (right) percentage of proliferating T cells (n = 5). B Percentage PD-1-positive T cells from (A), (n = 5). C Quantified small EV secretion in normoxia and hypoxia. The particle numbers were normalized over cell numbers (n = 3). D (Left) Volcano plot showing differentially expressed genes between normoxic and hypoxic RPMI-8226 myeloma cells. (Right) Bubble plot of significantly altered Wikipath pathways under hypoxic versus normoxic conditions. E CD45RO and CD62L expression in CD8+ BCMA CAR T cells, analyzed 48 h after small EV treatment (n = 4). Representative plots (top) and quantifications with different donors (bottom) are shown. F Cytotoxicity of RPMI-8226 cells after 24 h of co-culture (1:1 ratio) with anti-BCMA CAR T cells pretreated with either PBS (grey) or hypoxic sEVs (blue) (n = 3). P-values are indicated. Statistical significance was assessed using a one-way ANOVA for panels A and B, and a Student’s t-test for panels C and E. Experiments involving primary T cells (A, B,E, F) were performed using lymphocytes from at least three different healthy donors

body.p: In conclusion, we are the first to show that hypoxic myeloma cells exhibit reduced BCMA expression, rendering them less susceptible to BCMA-targeted CAR T cell therapy. Moreover, they secrete a more immunosuppressive secretome, including suppressive sEVs, that further impairs T cell functionality. While these results were obtained in vitro under controlled environments, they can most likely be applied to the in vivo situation where BCMA shedding is also observed within the (hypoxic) BM environment [11, 15]. Evaluating the impact of hypoxia and GSI treatment on CAR T therapy in vivo would be the next step in confirming this hypothesis.
